title: The groaning Spirit (Romans 8:26)
hookLine: when we don't know how to pray, the Spirit groans for us

cards: A car parked outside a sister's house, engine off. Someone behind the wheel means to pray before knocking. God, please.
Please what? Heal her? Give her peace?
Let it be quick? Every request sounds wrong the moment it forms. So no words come.
Just a long breath out, from somewhere under the ribs. Then they open the door and walk up the path. Was that a prayer?

teach.h: WE KNOW NOT WHAT TO PRAY FOR.
teach.b: Back on day one hundred six, a dry prayer still counted.

Here Paul goes further, in the King James words: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered."
Notice who admits not knowing. Not a beginner. Paul.
Not knowing how to pray isn't a failure here. It's assumed. And notice the sound: groanings which cannot be uttered.
Something deeper than words. In this one chapter, three things groan.

The first we met on the day about hope: the whole creation, groaning and travailing like a woman in labor. Then us: "even we ourselves groan within ourselves." And then the Spirit, groaning with us and for us.
The world aches, we ache, and God's own Spirit takes up the ache and carries it.
The next verse says the one who searches the hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, the same searching God of yesterday's psalm. Christians understand these groanings in different ways.
Some hear the Spirit's own wordless prayer, beyond anything we say. Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians connect this verse with praying in tongues; other Christians don't read it that way.
Whichever reading, the line keeps one comfort at its center: when words run out, the prayer doesn't. The breath in the parked car counts.

how: Christians lean on Romans 8:26 when they can't find words to pray, in grief or illness; some pray in silence, some sigh or weep before God, and some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians connect it with praying in tongues.

games.q: you're trying to pray for someone very sick, and every request you form sounds wrong. no words come. what does Romans 8 say happens?
o: nothing, until you find the right words.
the Spirit helps, with groanings which cannot be uttered.
the prayer doesn't count unless it's said aloud.
games.why: "the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered." in this chapter, running out of words is where the Spirit's help begins.

practice: Bring to mind the thing you don't know how to pray about, a person, or a situation with no good outcome you can name, and don't look for words.
Breathe in slowly and let it out as a long sigh with the weight of it inside, then once more.
If you pray, let the sigh be the prayer, trusting what Paul says about the Spirit carrying it; if you don't, let it simply be an honest breath that says this matters.
